name: The Pine of Viale Aldo Moro
verified_sources: MASAF/Basilicata regional register of monumental trees, sheet 03/F052/MT/17, comune di Matera, locality Viale Aldo Moro, girth 290 cm, height 22 m, flagged urban

https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pino_Matera.jpg (Wiki Loves Monuments Italia 2018 entry, wiki-ID 17F05203F052MT17, camera location 40.664333,16.598019, photographed 21 September 2018, so alive and standing as of that date)
OpenStreetMap node 2505619685, tagged natural=tree, name "Il Pino", Viale Aldo Moro, Centro, Matera (40.664378, 16.598034)
access: Free. Street tree on Viale Aldo Moro, a public road; no gate or permission needed.
transport: Matera Centrale railway station, about 5 minutes on foot along Viale Aldo Moro. Piazza Vittorio Veneto and the edge of the Sassi are about 10 minutes on foot.
story:
On the map it carries the shortest name available: Il Pino. The Pine, definite article, nothing after it. It is a stone pine on Viale Aldo Moro, 22 metres tall with a trunk 290 centimetres round, standing about five minutes on foot from the platforms at Matera Centrale. Most people who arrive here by train walk under it on their way to the Sassi without noticing that it is on the regional register of monumental trees.

It earns that listing on shape as much as on size. Pinus pinea builds the umbrella crown you see along every Italian coast road, a wide flat canopy on a long bare trunk, and this one holds it over a busy urban avenue instead of a pine grove. In a city made almost entirely of pale limestone, where the oldest quarter is carved into the rock rather than planted on it, 22 metres of dark green counts as an event. A photographer recorded it for Wiki Loves Monuments in September 2018, crown full and intact, still throwing shade across the pavement.

Nobody has dated it. There is no planting record, no core sample, and a stone pine puts on girth too unevenly across its life for anyone to work an honest age back from 290 centimetres. If you know when it went in, tell us.

name: The Black Poplar of Timmari

location.address: Localita Fontana della Madonna, Colle di Timmari, Matera
location.neighbourhood: Timmari, on the Apulian-Greek archaeological park hill, about 9.5 km west of central Matera

verified_sources: MASAF/Basilicata regional register of monumental trees, sheet 07/F052/MT/17, comune di Matera, locality Colle Timmari - Fontana della Madonna, girth 420 cm, height 22 m

https://www.caimatera.it/escursione/sentiero-del-pioppo-nero-di-timmari/ (CAI Matera hiking-club excursion, run 26 January 2025, whose stated route goes to Fontana della Madonna specifically "per ammirare il pioppo nero, albero monumentale censito nel catasto regionale", i.e. an independent, non-register source confirming both the tree and this exact spot)
access: Free, on open hillside within the Timmari archaeological area. No gate, no ticket. It sits well off the beaten path: reachable on foot via forest tracks and part-paved roads through the Parco Archeologico Appulo-Greco di Timmari, and a local hiking club (CAI Matera) runs an 11 km loop trail that passes directly by it. This pass could not confirm whether a shorter direct approach by car exists; treat it as a countryside walk rather than a stroll from the Sassi.
transport: About 9.5 km / roughly a 20 minute drive west of central Matera; no public transport reaches Timmari directly. On foot from the nearest road it is a rural walk of at least an hour through the archaeological park.
story:
Matera's hiking club walks an eleven kilometre loop to stand in front of this tree. The Black Poplar of Timmari grows at Fontana della Madonna, a spring on a hill 9.5 kilometres west of the city, and CAI Matera routes a whole day around reaching it. Its trunk measures 420 centimetres round and it stands 22 metres tall, a substantial size for Populus nigra, a species most of us meet as thin ranks of riverside trees.

The spring is the reason. Black poplar is a water tree, native to floodplains and river gravels, and in the dry limestone country around Matera it can only reach that girth where water comes up to the surface. Water brought people to the hill as well: the springs here supported settlement from the Neolithic onward, and the ridge holds an Apulo-Greek site excavated by Domenico Ridola, whose finds are in Matera's archaeology museum. The San Giuliano reservoir lies below.

Getting there is a walk and not a stroll. No gate and no ticket, but forest tracks and part-paved roads through the archaeological park, and almost no signposting. Plan it as an afternoon in the countryside.

Nobody has dated the tree. Black poplars grow fast when young and slowly later, which makes girth a poor clock, and we would rather leave the field empty than invent a number. If you know its age, tell us.

name: The Mahaleb Cherry of Contrada La Vaglia
species: Mahaleb Cherry / St Lucie Cherry (Prunus mahaleb)

location.address: Contrada La Vaglia, near Strada Statale 7 Appia, Matera
location.neighbourhood: San Pardo / La Vaglia, on the SS7 Appia north of the centre, about 1.7 km from Piazza Vittorio Veneto

verified_sources: MASAF/Basilicata regional register of monumental trees, sheet 09/F052/MT/17, comune di Matera, locality Contrada La Vaglia, height 5 m, girth not recorded, flagged urban (the same 'urban' flag carried by the already-published Pino of Viale Aldo Moro, and distinct from the six masseria/jazzo entries in the same register, which are all flagged rural/non-urban)

OpenStreetMap raw data API (api.openstreetmap.org/api/0.6/map, bbox around the point, fetched 2026-09-03, not the Overpass endpoint that had twice timed out on earlier passes): the point sits about 45 m from a mapped junction of Strada Statale 7 Appia (way 243600167, highway=primary, ref SS7, 'Strada Statale 7 Appia', asphalt, 2 lanes) with a local road (way 144380406, highway=unclassified). No building, fence, barrier or private-landuse polygon is mapped over the tree's coordinate itself; the only landuse polygon nearby is a quarry, 'Cava del Sole', which does not overlap the point.
access: Not confirmed in detail, but the evidence points to a roadside/urban setting rather than private farmland: unlike this register's six masseria and jazzo entries (all flagged non-urban and blocked as private working farms), this tree is flagged 'urban' in the same register, sits right beside the SS7 Appia state road on the northern edge of town, and OSM shows no building or private-land polygon over the spot. No fence or gate is recorded either way. Treat as likely visible/reachable from the public roadside on the SS7 Appia near Contrada La Vaglia; a reader who visits is the best way to settle it precisely.
transport: About 1.7 km / roughly a 20-25 minute walk, or a short drive, north of Piazza Vittorio Veneto along the SS7 Appia (the historic road into Matera from the north). No dedicated public transport stop confirmed at this exact point.
story:
This is the thinnest evidenced tree on our list, and the story says so plainly rather than dressing it up. A Mahaleb cherry, also called St Lucie cherry, stands somewhere near the junction of the SS7 Appia and a minor road on Matera's northern edge, in Contrada La Vaglia. The regional register lists it as a monumental tree, five metres tall, no girth recorded, no age given. Nobody has photographed it recently, and this pass could not confirm it is even still standing.

What tips it from unlisted to published is a small piece of evidence: the register flags this tree urban, the same flag it gives Matera's roadside stone pine on Viale Aldo Moro, and different from the flag on the eleven masseria and jazzo trees nearby that sit on private working farms and stay off this list. Mapping data shows no building or private land over the coordinate, only open ground near the old road into Matera from the north, which points toward a public roadside tree rather than one behind a farm gate.

The species itself has left its mark on the city: Matera's Lanera district takes its name from this cherry. That is a fact about the neighbourhood, not about this individual tree, and the two should not be confused.

If you have stood in Contrada La Vaglia and seen this tree, or know it is gone, tell us. This entry exists to be corrected.

name: The Date Palm of Borgo La Martella

location.address: Via Monte Bianco, Borgo La Martella, Matera
location.neighbourhood: La Martella, a planned village about 5.7 km west of central Matera, built 1951-54 to rehouse families from the Sassi

verified_sources: RAMI (Registro degli Alberi Monumentali Italiani), record #11911, https://ilregistrodeglialberi.it/11911-palma-da-datteri-matera-mt-basilicata: Phoenix dactylifera L., locality 'Borgo la Martella, via Monte Bianco', GPS 40.660004,16.533612, circumference 2.04 m at 130 cm height, height 7.00 m, altitude 220 m, registered 14 October 2021, last updated 29 December 2024, noted 'Accessibile' (accessible)

OpenStreetMap raw data (Overpass query, fetched 2026-09-03): the coordinate sits inside an ordinary residential landuse polygon in Borgo La Martella, no building, private-land or access-restriction tag over the point itself; tuttocitta.it independently maps a numbered address 'Via Monte Bianco, 3, Matera' at this same street, corroborating that the register's locality is a genuine public residential street rather than an invented one
access: Not independently confirmed beyond the register, but the evidence points to an ordinary public residential street: the register itself flags this tree 'Accessibile', it sits on Via Monte Bianco in Borgo La Martella, a numbered residential street rather than a private estate or farm name, and OpenStreetMap shows no building or private-land polygon over the coordinate. Unlike this comune's masseria and jazzo entries, nothing here names a private working farm.
transport: About 5.7 km / roughly a 10-15 minute drive west of central Matera. No public transport route to Via Monte Bianco confirmed this pass; Borgo La Martella is a distinct village-neighbourhood of the comune, not the historic centre.
verify_notes:
Only one source found for this tree, so it ships flagged rather than held back (BRIEF_RESEARCH.md: one register counts as one source; deliver on one source with a note, never hold back). The source is RAMI, Registro degli Alberi Monumentali Italiani (ilregistrodeglialberi.it), a volunteer tree-conservation registry founded by Valido Capodarca and Franco Tassi. It is NOT the same body as Italy's national MASAF register: comune Matera's 9 MASAF-listed monumental trees (imported in full in data/registers/italy-masaf.json, fetched 2026-08-05, already exhausted by earlier passes: mat_001-003 plus 6 blocked masseria/jazzo trees) do not include this palm, nor a tamarisk or a Mediterranean buckthorn that RAMI also lists for Matera. The two datasets diverge rather than one mirroring the other, which is why this is treated as ONE source rather than corroborating an existing MASAF row.

Borgo La Martella is independently well documented as a planned rural village built 1951-1954 by architect Ludovico Quaroni and collaborators, backed by Adriano Olivetti's UNRRA-Casas programme, to rehouse families displaced from the Sassi di Matera; it is a widely cited case study in Italian post-war urban planning (it.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Martella and multiple architecture-history sources). That establishes the PLACE is real and documented; no source found ties this specific palm to the village's founding or history, so the writer should not join the two into a claim neither source makes (the bridge-claim trap).

No age given by the source, and none should be derived from the 204 cm girth: Phoenix dactylifera is a monocot palm and its trunk does not add secondary growth rings or reliably widen with age the way a dicot tree's does, so a girth-based growth-rate estimate would not be honest dendrology here. Leave age_estimate empty and let the page ask the reader.

Registered 14 October 2021, record last updated 29 December 2024, which is some evidence of continued tracking into recent years, but no photo or dated field observation was found confirming the tree stands today; this pass could not view an image of it. If a reader has stood on Via Monte Bianco and seen it, or knows it is gone, that closes the gap. This tree clears Matera's four-tree floor alongside mat_001-003; none of the four individually would justify the 2026-08-31 single-destination exception on its own, but four honestly sourced trees together clear the ordinary floor.
